title: A Graft Changes Its Neighbours' Fate

scenes.tts: Take a small piece of tissue from one newt embryo. Place it in the side of another. The host builds a second neural tube. Where do the cells of that tube come from? The answer shows how one tissue can change the fate of its neighbours.
scenes.visual: A donor embryo gives up a patch that is moved into a host; a second tube of cells marked with question marks appears; two chips ask graft cells or host cells.
scenes.narration: Take a small piece of tissue from one newt embryo. Place it in the side of another. The host builds a second neural tube. Where do the cells of that tube come from? The answer shows how one tissue can change the fate of its neighbours.

scenes.tts: Early in development, the embryo sorts itself into three layers. The outer layer, the ectoderm, makes outer skin and the nervous system. A strip of ectoderm along the back, the neural plate, rolls up into the neural tube. Ectoderm on the belly becomes skin. Both start as the same kind of surface tissue. So what is different? Underneath the back, cells that rolled inward over the dorsal lip form the mesoderm.
scenes.visual: Three rows of cells; the ectoderm row turns blue, the back strip turns purple and rolls into a tube, belly cells stay skin, mesoderm slides in under the back over the dorsal lip.
scenes.narration: Early in development, the embryo sorts itself into three layers. The outer layer, the ectoderm, makes outer skin and the nervous system. A strip of ectoderm along the back, the neural plate, rolls up into the neural tube. Ectoderm on the belly becomes skin. Both start as the same kind of surface tissue. So what is different? Underneath the back, cells that rolled inward over the dorsal lip form the mesoderm.

scenes.tts: Hilde Mangold used two newt species. Cells of one carry little pigment, so they look pale. Cells of the other carry pigment granules. The granules stay visible in thin sections. She cut a small piece of dorsal lip from a pale embryo. She placed it in the belly of a pigmented embryo, in tissue that would become belly skin.
scenes.visual: A pale donor strip and a dotted pigmented host strip; a patch is cut from the donor lip and tucked under the host belly ectoderm.
scenes.narration: Hilde Mangold used two newt species. Cells of one carry little pigment, so they look pale. Cells of the other carry pigment granules. The granules stay visible in thin sections. She cut a small piece of dorsal lip from a pale embryo. She placed it in the belly of a pigmented embryo, in tissue that would become belly skin.

scenes.tts: A second neural plate rose beside the host's own. It folded, and closed into a second neural tube. In thin sections, most of that tube was pigmented. So it was made of host cells. A narrow pale strip from the graft lay along its floor. In another embryo, the whole tube was host tissue. The pale graft lay beneath it, as a second notochord.
scenes.visual: Host ectoderm over the graft turns purple, folds into a tube; a section shows dotted host cells with a pale floor strip, then an all-dotted tube above a pale notochord.
scenes.narration: A second neural plate rose beside the host's own. It folded, and closed into a second neural tube. In thin sections, most of that tube was pigmented. So it was made of host cells. A narrow pale strip from the graft lay along its floor. In another embryo, the whole tube was host tissue. The pale graft lay beneath it, as a second notochord.

scenes.tts: Host ectoderm that would have made skin had made nervous system instead. This is induction. Induction is a change in the fate of one tissue, caused by a signal from another. The responding tissue must be able to answer. That ability is called competence. It does not last. In amphibians, ectoderm from older embryos responds less and less.
scenes.visual: Blue ectoderm turns purple under a yellow signal from a signaling tissue; competence is tagged on the responder; a response curve falls with the age of the ectoderm.
scenes.narration: Host ectoderm that would have made skin had made nervous system instead. This is induction. Induction is a change in the fate of one tissue, caused by a signal from another. The responding tissue must be able to answer. That ability is called competence. It does not last. In amphibians, ectoderm from older embryos responds less and less.

scenes.tts: The dorsal lip is called the organizer. Its signals do more than switch on one fate. Its own cells become notochord. It recruits neighbouring mesoderm into dorsal fates. And it induces the ectoderm. The graft left one question open: what is the signal? Keep the rule: a cell's fate depends, in part, on the signals it receives.
scenes.visual: The organizer block sends three arrows: to a notochord chip, to neighbouring mesoderm, to ectoderm that turns purple; then a question mark on the signal and the rule.
